content: Support for pregnant adolescents transitioning into adult healthcare services is infrequent. Approximately 46% of respondents reported that their facilities address the specific needs of HIV-infected pregnant adolescents. These services include prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), antenatal care (ANC), management as special cases, support groups for HIV-infected pregnant adolescents, general counseling, social services, and grants assistance. Sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services are provided to HIV-infected adolescents in 63% of facilities. East African facilities are more likely to offer these services (84%) compared to Southern African facilities (68%) and West and Central African facilities, where 73% do not provide SRH services. The most common SRH services include family planning and contraceptives (72%), general counseling and health education (40%), and sexually transmitted infection (STI) screening and treatment (31%). Cervical cancer screening is offered in only 14% of facilities, while PMTCT, ANC, and voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) are each provided in 10% of facilities. Transitioning HIV-infected pregnant adolescents to adult services often occurs without adequate preparation or support. Healthcare providers report that pregnancy is a key factor in transitioning adolescents out of pediatric or adolescent services. For example, a nurse in Namibia explained that adolescents are counseled about transitioning based on age or pregnancy, making the process easier as they are already aware of the criteria. A doctor in Uganda noted that pregnant adolescents are often moved to adult services to avoid harassment from peers and to help them focus on caring for their baby. However, a doctor in Malawi highlighted that many adolescents default on care due to the lack of a structured transition process. HIV services for adolescents are fully integrated in only 46% of facilities, partially integrated in 43%, and not integrated at all in 11%. Community integration and referral networks are also limited, with 57% of respondents reporting relationships with non-governmental organizations (NGOs), 52% with community-based organizations (CBOs), and 20% with faith-based organizations (FBOs). However, 16% of facilities reported having no external relationships. Data collection for adolescents is inconsistent. Only 66% of facilities identify adolescents in their records, and age-disaggregated data is not consistently collected. Additionally, 80% of facilities do not record treatment outcomes specifically for adolescents. This lack of data hinders research, policy development, and the identification of best practices for adolescent HIV care. Adherence and retention challenges are significant. In 45% of facilities, there is no clear method to determine adherence, and over a third lack guidelines for managing adolescents with adherence difficulties. Only 67% of facilities provide services to improve treatment adherence, and less than two-thirds offer services to support retention in care. Peer support activities and clubs are the most common approach to addressing adherence and retention issues, but not all facilities offer these services. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of peer-based interventions and to address systemic barriers. The transition from pediatric to adult services typically occurs at 18 years of age, but only 35% of facilities provide separate services for adolescents. Transition-specific counseling is offered in 63% of facilities, but the content and participants in these sessions vary widely. Guidelines for transitioning are present in only half of the facilities. The lack of standardized transition processes and adolescent-specific services highlights the need for revised guidelines to ensure high-quality care during this critical period. West and Central Africa lag behind other regions in providing adolescent-specific HIV services, with only 7% of facilities offering separate services and 42% not tracking treatment outcomes. East Africa leads in having guidelines, processes, and systems in place for adolescent care, with facilities in this region being almost twice as likely to offer adherence support compared to West and Central Africa. The findings underscore the urgent need for standardized definitions of adolescence, improved data collection, and comprehensive SRH services for HIV-infected adolescents. These measures are essential to address the unique challenges faced by this population and to inform global HIV response strategies.
